proposal.utterance: What BFO category best fits 'the normative force of an obligation'?

entities.label: NormativeForce
entities.rationale: Normative force is the capacity or potency of an obligation to bind, direct, or compel action. It is internally grounded in the obligation bearer (the person or entity that holds the obligation) and is not merely an externally assigned label. This makes it a Disposition (BFO_0000016) rather than a Quality: it is a realizable entity that is manifested when the obligated agent acts (or fails to act) in response to the norm. It inheres in the bearer of the obligation (a person or legal entity), and is realized in processes of compliance, enforcement, or deliberation. It is distinct from the obligation itself (already modeled as working:LegalObligation, a Role subclass), which is the social/relational structure; normative force is the causal-dispositional aspect that drives or grounds the 'oughtness' felt or recognized by the bearer.

relations.rationale: NormativeForce is a subclass of Disposition (BFO_0000016): it is an internally grounded realizable that inheres in a bearer and is realized in processes of norm-compliance or norm-enforcement.
Disposition is itself a subclass of Specifically Dependent Continuant (BFO_0000020), so NormativeForce inherits this typing; making it explicit supports reasoning.

open_questions: Should NormativeForce be restricted to legal obligations only (subclass of a disposition inhering in bearers of working:LegalObligation), or should it be general enough to cover moral and other normative obligations as well?

Is the intent to model normative force as a property of the obligation-instance (the role inhering in a person), or as a property of the norm-content (the generically dependent continuant, e.g., a statute)? The answer shifts the bearer: if the former, it inheres in a person; if the latter, it would need a different BFO anchor.

Should 'normative force' be distinguished from 'obligatory force' (the specific force of an obligation) versus 'permissive force' or 'prohibitory force'? If so, NormativeForce could be a parent class with more specific subclasses.
Is there an interest in also modeling the process in which normative force is realized (e.g., a compliance act, an enforcement act) as a subclass of BFO_0000015 (Process)?
proposal.rationale_summary: The normative force of an obligation is best typed as a Disposition (BFO_0000016) under BFO 2020. A Disposition is a specifically dependent continuant that is internally grounded in its bearer and is realized in processes. Normative force fits this profile: it is the potency or bindingness that inheres in the agent who bears an obligation and is realized when that agent deliberates, complies, or is held accountable. It is not a Quality (BFO_0000019) because it is not a static measurable attribute but a directed capacity; it is not a Role (BFO_0000023) because it is not externally conferred by social recognition but arises from the structural features of the normative relationship itself. The existing working:LegalObligation class already models the obligation as a role (externally grounded relational property); NormativeForce is proposed as a complementary Disposition class capturing the internal-to-bearer, causally efficacious aspect of that same normative relationship. A new class working:NormativeForce rdfs:subClassOf BFO_0000016 is proposed, with open questions about scope, bearer, and further specialization left for the user to resolve.
